prompt: A listing broker's primary fiduciary duty to the seller client is to:

options.text: Promote the seller's interests with loyalty, care, and obedience within the law
Obtain the highest possible price even when the seller directs a quicker sale
Treat buyer and seller with equal advocacy so both receive fair representation
Advise the seller on title and tax matters as the seller's legal representative

explanation: Agency duties center on loyalty and obedience to lawful client instructions, not guaranteeing outcomes.

distractorExplanations.b: Price is not the top duty; obedience requires following the seller's lawful instruction to favor a quick sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal advocacy describes a neutral or dual role; a listing broker owes loyalty to the seller client, not both sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses agency with legal practice; a broker must refer title and tax questions to an attorney or CPA.

prompt: When must a licensee typically disclose a dual agency or designated agency relationship?

Before or as soon as practicable when the dual/designated relationship arises
Once the purchase contract is accepted and both parties have signed it
Only if one of the parties is an existing client rather than a customer

explanation: Agency disclosure timing is early—when the dual or designated relationship is created or contemplated. Exact timing follows the applicable license-law rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Closing is far too late; informed consent must come before the licensee acts for both parties.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting until acceptance means both parties negotiated without knowing the licensee's divided loyalty.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure is triggered by the dual or designated relationship itself, not by whether a party was a prior client.

prompt: An exclusive right-to-sell listing generally means:

The listing broker is owed a commission if the property sells during the term, regardless of who finds the buyer

explanation: Exclusive right-to-sell typically protects the listing broker's commission if a sale occurs during the listing term. The exact protection follows the terms of the listing agreement.

distractorExplanations.b: That describes an open listing, where only the procuring broker is paid and the seller may also sell directly.

prompt: A Maine purchase falls apart after the inspection. The buyer demands his $10,000 earnest money back; the seller claims it as damages. The broker holds the funds in escrow, and neither party will sign a release. What is the broker's best course?

options.text: Hold the funds and, if the dispute persists, file an interpleader action
Release the money to the seller, because the seller is the broker's own client
Split the deposit 50/50 between the parties as a fair compromise
Keep the deposit as the commission earned on the failed transaction

explanation: Earnest money held in escrow belongs to neither side until the parties agree in writing or a court decides. When buyer and seller both claim it, the broker should keep it in the trust account and may file an interpleader, depositing the money with the court so a judge decides who gets it, which also protects the broker from liability.

distractorExplanations.b: Representing the seller does not let the broker decide a contract dispute; releasing escrow without both signatures or an order invites liability.
distractorExplanations.c: The broker has no authority to impose a compromise; a split requires written agreement from both parties or a court order.
distractorExplanations.d: Escrowed earnest money is not the broker's to keep; commission is owed under the listing, not taken from disputed trust funds.

prompt: A net listing arrangement is often risky or restricted because

prompt: A Maine buyer pays cash for a cottage without ordering a title search. Weeks later a bank produces a mortgage the prior owner gave in 2019, properly recorded and never paid off. The buyer says he had no idea it existed. What is the result?

options.text: The mortgage is void against him because he had no actual knowledge
The mortgage is unenforceable because the buyer paid cash at closing
The bank must collect from the prior owner and cannot reach the cottage
He takes subject to the lien; recording gave him constructive notice

explanation: Recording a document in the public land records gives constructive notice to everyone, whether or not they actually look. A buyer is treated as knowing whatever a proper title search would have revealed. The 2019 mortgage was recorded, so the lien stays on the cottage; the buyer's remedy is against the seller under the deed's warranties or under title insurance, if any.

distractorExplanations.a: Actual knowledge is not required; a recorded document binds later buyers through constructive notice even if they never searched.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying cash does not cut off a recorded lien; the mortgage attaches to the property, not to the buyer's method of payment.
distractorExplanations.c: A recorded mortgage is a lien on the property itself, so the bank can foreclose on the cottage even after it changes hands.

prompt: A Maine buyer gets seller financing of $96,000 at 7.5%, with interest-only monthly payments and the full principal due in 24 months. What is the final balloon payment, including that month's interest?

options.text: $600 at month 24

$110,400 at month 24
